Project Mode.Purpose: Tracks pipeline runs for one compartment over time, so you do not pick every input file by hand between stages. A project holds one baseline, zero or more scans, and zero or more diffs.
Project Mode.Baseline: The first scan of a compartment. A project has exactly one baseline. Stage 1, 2, 3, and 4 (SLAM, Level, Cleanup, Segment) run once for the baseline.
Project Mode.Scans: Later scans of the same compartment, done to check for new damage. Each scan runs its own Stage 1, 2, 3, and 4. Add a scan with the 'New Scan' button. A scan needs its own raw source file, separate from the baseline's.
Project Mode.Diffs: A comparison between two cleanup outputs. Each diff runs Stage 5, 6, 7, and 8 (Diff, Classify, Surface, Export). A diff can compare a scan against the baseline, or against an earlier scan - so the same scan can show total change since the baseline, and separately, change since the last check. A diff's own M3C2 comparison (Stage 5) lets you pick, for each side, between that side's Stage 3 (Cleanup) output and its Stage 4 (Segment) classified output, via 'Choose from project...' - either is valid input, since Segment only adds a classification field on top of the same points. Add a diff with the 'New Diff' button.
Project Mode.Pipeline selectors: Two dropdowns near the top of the main window pick which pipeline the stage buttons act on. 'Source pipeline' picks the baseline or a scan, for Stage 1, 2, 3, and 4. 'Diff pipeline' picks a diff, for Stage 5, 6, 7, and 8. The status label next to them shows each picked pipeline's next stage.
Project Mode.Manual mode: Every stage dialog also works with no project open. Browse to input files by hand, same as before project mode existed. No project.json file is written in manual mode. There is no separate 'manual override' setting inside a dialog anymore - a project-mode input field starts blank either way, and can be filled by typing, Browse..., or (when a project pipeline is active) the 'Choose from project...' picker - all three just fill the same field.

Stage 1: SLAM.Purpose: Builds a 3D point cloud map and computes sensor trajectory poses from a raw lidar capture. Two backend options: Ouster CLI (reads raw sensor packets directly) or KISS-ICP (a different algorithm entry point, reads already-decoded PointCloud2 rosbag topics directly - works even when Ouster CLI can't read the same bag, since it doesn't need raw packets).
Stage 1: SLAM.Inputs:
- Backend: Ouster CLI or KISS-ICP
- Source: a .pcap capture, an .osf file, a ROS1 .bag file, or a ROS2 bag folder (containing .db3 + metadata.yaml) - both backends auto-detect the type. Starts blank; type, browse, or (in project mode) use 'Choose from project...' to pick the pipeline's raw imported source (the baseline's, or a scan's - original or decoded, if a decoded copy exists). Picking a ROS2 bag folder here also checks it for raw Ouster packets - see What to expect.
- Meta JSON file (required for Ouster CLI + .pcap, optional/backend-dependent otherwise)
- [Ouster CLI] Voxel size in meters, visualizer toggle
- [KISS-ICP] Config .yaml (strongly recommended - see What to expect), optional voxel size override, optional min range override (see What to expect - useful when the sensor sees part of its own mount), optional dataloader/topic overrides
Stage 1: SLAM.Outputs: A single .ply point cloud map, saved to the path you choose. In project mode, this run's result is recorded on whichever pipeline is picked under 'Source pipeline' (the baseline, or the picked scan) - not on any other scan.
Stage 1: SLAM.What to expect:
Processing time scales with capture length. The map's orientation is arbitrary either way - neither backend has a gravity/leveling step, so the map inherits whatever tilt the sensor had at the very first frame. That's expected, not a bug - Stage 2 (Level) corrects it.

KISS-ICP specifically: without a config file, its defaults assume vehicle-scale outdoor odometry (max_range=100m) - confirmed on real data to under-populate an indoor map by roughly 190x (2,628 points vs. 503,189 points on the same capture, with vs. without a properly scaled config). The KISS-ICP config field defaults to the bundled 'kiss_icp_config_indoor.yaml' (already tuned for this project's compartment scale) if it's sitting next to the applet - double check it hasn't been accidentally swapped for a ROS bag's own metadata.yaml, a different file that happens to share the same common filename. Both per-point deskewing and sensor calibration have been separately verified correct when reading PointCloud2 rosbag topics - the point-count issue is purely the default config scale, not a data-quality problem.

KISS-ICP min range override: a robot-mounted sensor can see part of its own mount hardware. This can happen on a stable platform just as much as an unstable one - platform stability affects drift, not this. Each of these near-sensor points sits at the same spot next to the sensor in every single frame. Added together, they can form a dense, solid-looking blob of noise near the sensor in the final map. They can also confuse the SLAM solver: the solver may read this fixed, unmoving blob as real unmoving geometry, and align each frame to it instead of to the room. This can show up as a map that looks noisy, or as a map with the wrong shape. The min range override removes points closer than the set distance, before SLAM runs. Start with a small value, for example 0.2 to 0.3 meters, and raise it only as far as needed - a value set too high also removes real nearby room detail, not just mount noise. The 'This config's own min_range' label shows the current config file's own value, so you can tell whether a run used a value from the config or your own override.

Picking a ROS2 bag folder as Source checks its metadata.yaml for a decoded PointCloud2 topic. Some captures record raw Ouster sensor packets instead, to save bandwidth on the Jetson during capture and transfer - KISS-ICP needs a PointCloud2 topic and cannot read raw packets directly. If the check finds raw packets and no PointCloud2 topic, the dialog asks you to confirm a conversion, regardless of which Backend is selected - Ouster CLI can already read raw packets directly, but a decoded copy is still offered since it stays useful for comparing backends side by side or for use outside this pipeline. On yes, it runs decode_raw_packets.py; once the run finishes with no error, it fills the Source field with the decoded bag directly - and, if a project pipeline is active, also records the decoded path on that pipeline, so it shows up as a 'decoded' option under 'Choose from project...' next time too. A 'Check Source for Raw Packets...' button next to the field runs the same check by hand, for a path typed in instead of browsed to. This conversion step has been confirmed working end to end against real hardware data: a real capture decoded 748 scans from 47,906 lidar packets with 0 packets skipped.
Stage 1: SLAM.Next steps: Take it into Stage 2 (Level) to correct any tilt before cleanup. Both backends can point at the same source with different output filenames, for side-by-side comparison of map quality.

Stage 2: Level.Purpose: Corrects the SLAM map's arbitrary tilt so the floor is horizontal and sits at Z=0. It finds the floor plane with RANSAC, then rotates the cloud to match.
Stage 2: Level.Inputs:
- Raw SLAM output .ply (starts blank; use 'Choose from project...' to pick Stage 1's output, in project mode)
- Output .ply path
- Distance threshold, max planes to search, min plane size - the RANSAC tuning knobs
- Horizontal threshold - how close to vertical a plane must be to count as floor/ceiling at all (see What to expect)
Stage 2: Level.Outputs: A leveled .ply, rotated so the detected floor plane is horizontal and translated so it sits at Z=0.
Stage 2: Level.What to expect: The tool output lists every candidate plane found, its height (Z position), and whether it cleared the horizontal threshold. The floor is picked as the LOWEST candidate that clears this threshold, not the biggest one - a real ceiling can have more points than a real floor (a cleaner surface, with less clutter on it), so picking by size alone can pick the ceiling by mistake. If the chosen floor has very few points, or the console shows a low-horizontality warning or a fallback warning (no candidate cleared the threshold at all), check the result visually in CloudCompare before trusting it.
Stage 2: Level.Next steps: Open the leveled cloud in CloudCompare to confirm the floor genuinely looks horizontal now. Then use it as the input to Stage 3 (Cleanup).

Stage 3: Cleanup.Purpose: Removes noisy outlier points from a raw SLAM map using Statistical Outlier Removal (SOR), and optionally fine-aligns it onto a baseline map with ICP to correct residual drift.
Stage 3: Cleanup.Inputs:
- Input .ply to clean (starts blank; use 'Choose from project...' to pick Stage 2's output, in project mode)
- SOR neighbor count and standard deviation threshold
- Optional: baseline .ply to align onto. In project mode, if the picked pipeline is a scan, a 'Use Project Baseline' button fills this from the project's own baseline cleanup output - the usual choice, since a later 'vs. baseline' diff needs this scan aligned to the real baseline. Manual mode still has its own separate registered-baseline dropdown.
- Output .ply path (you choose this - CloudCompare saves exactly there)
- Optional: also register this output as a manual-mode baseline for a compartment name (a separate mechanism from a project's own baseline - see What to expect)
Stage 3: Cleanup.Outputs: A cleaned .ply file at the exact path you chose. If alignment ran, CloudCompare also resaves a throwaway copy of the baseline in the same folder (a CloudCompare CLI limitation, not an extra result to worry about) and auto-generates a registration log .txt (RMS, transformation matrix, point counts). In project mode, the RMS value and the RMS sidecar's path are also recorded directly on this pipeline's cleanup stage entry.
Stage 3: Cleanup.What to expect:
CloudCompare names the output file itself when it runs (its own auto-naming, not a filename you chose) - the applet detects whatever new .ply appeared after the run and renames it to the path you asked for. An earlier version tried to force an exact filename directly via a CloudCompare flag, but that proved unreliable in real testing (inconsistent in both directions across separate runs) - this detect-and-rename approach replaced it and has held up in testing since.

'Register this output as a manual-mode baseline' and a project's own baseline are two different things. A project's baseline is the project's own record, tracked in that project's project.json - nothing extra to register. The manual-mode registry (baseline_registry.json) is a separate, standalone lookup that only matters when no project is open.
Stage 3: Cleanup.Next steps: Open the cleaned .ply in CloudCompare to confirm the alignment looks right, and check the RMS in the registration log - lower is better. If this output IS a compartment's baseline (nothing to align it to), that project's baseline pipeline already IS the record that matters - no extra step needed.

Stage 4: Segment.Purpose: Classifies a cleaned cloud's own points into floor, ceiling, individual walls, and unclassified, using segment_planes.py - the same RANSAC plane-finding approach Stage 2 (Level) uses, extended to keep every detected surface rather than just the floor. Runs once per baseline/scan pipeline, right after Cleanup - not per diff, since it describes ONE cloud's own structure, not a comparison between two clouds. Stage 5 (Diff) can use this stage's classified output for a side instead of Stage 3's cleanup output, picked explicitly via 'Choose from project...'.
Stage 4: Segment.Inputs:
- Cleaned .ply, ideally leveled first (starts blank; use 'Choose from project...' to pick Stage 3's output, in project mode)
- Distance threshold, max planes, min plane size, horizontal threshold, max horizontal Z span - the same RANSAC tuning knobs Stage 2 (Level) exposes, plus two extra ones this stage needs since it keeps every surface, not just the floor
- Stray-point cluster filter (on by default) and its gap tolerance / minimum point count
- Split-plane merge (on by default) and its normal-similarity / distance tolerances
- 'Also write each surface as its own separate .ply file' checkbox, off by default (see Outputs)
- 'Flag unclassified points that sit outside the room as junk' checkbox, on by default, its margin field, and an 'Also write a separate copy with outside-envelope points removed' checkbox, off by default (see What to expect)
- Output folder (not a single file - see Outputs)
Stage 4: Segment.Outputs: Written into one folder. By default, only a combined <name>_classified.ply (every input point, carrying a 'classification' field naming which surface it belongs to, an 'is_envelope' field, and an 'outside_envelope' field - see What to expect), a <name>_envelope.ply (the classified surfaces only, no interior/clutter - a ready-made input for Stage 7/Surface's unified shell reconstruction), and a manifest.json summarizing both. '<name>' is the output folder's own name, so files from different runs stay distinguishable even when opened outside their own folder. Turn on 'Also write each surface as its own separate .ply file' to also get one cloud per detected surface (<name>_floor.ply, <name>_ceiling.ply, <name>_wall_1.ply, and so on) and a <name>_unclassified.ply (points that matched no surface) written alongside those - useful for visually tuning parameters per surface, or so each surface becomes its own separate object in Omniverse. Turn on 'Also write a separate copy with outside-envelope points removed' to also get <name>_envelope_filtered.ply - the combined cloud with junk points removed (see What to expect). In project mode, this stage's recorded 'output' is <name>_classified.ply specifically; the envelope path, the surface list, the classification ID mapping, and the outside-envelope filter's own results are recorded directly on this pipeline's segment stage entry, the same way Stage 3's RMS gets copied in - manifest.json does not need to be read separately once a run is recorded.
Stage 4: Segment.What to expect:
The floor/ceiling/wall classification is a straightforward height-and-orientation heuristic, not a tuned one - if a wall gets misclassified as ceiling or vice versa, check it against the surface list in the run report. If a real wall seems to be missing, turn on the separate-surfaces checkbox and re-run, then check the <name>_unclassified.ply cloud for a flat-ish cluster of points rather than a scattered one - that is usually the missing wall, broken up by clutter or debris stuck to it, not lost data. You can also check <name>_classified.ply's own 'classification' field (0 = unclassified) without turning that checkbox on at all.

Outside-envelope junk filter: every point classified as floor, ceiling, or a wall already describes the room's own shape. Any point NOT classified as one of those - the 'unclassified' points - can be real interior clutter or damage, or it can be scan noise from beyond the walls. This filter checks each unclassified point against the room's own footprint (worked out from the detected floor/ceiling/wall points) and height range, with some margin for slack near real walls. A point that falls outside both counts as likely junk and gets a new 'outside_envelope' field set to 1 in <name>_classified.ply. A point that falls inside keeps 'outside_envelope' at 0 - this covers both real interior clutter and every detected surface's own points. No point is ever removed from <name>_classified.ply because of this field - it is a label, added so you can filter or color by it later, not a deletion. Raise the margin field if real clutter near a wall is getting flagged by mistake; lower it if real junk near a wall is getting missed. If the run report says the filter was skipped, not enough floor/ceiling/wall surface was detected that run to work out a room footprint at all - check the surface list first.
Stage 4: Segment.Next steps: Open <name>_classified.ply in CloudCompare and color by the 'classification' field to confirm the surfaces look right. Color by 'outside_envelope' to check the junk filter's flags before trusting them - if real content is getting flagged, raise the margin and re-run. Use <name>_envelope.ply as the input to Stage 7 (Surface) for a single unified shell reconstruction across floor/ceiling/walls together, instead of reconstructing each one as a separate disconnected mesh patch.

Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Purpose: Runs M3C2 (multiscale model-to-model cloud comparison) to compute point-level distances between two clouds, highlighting where a compartment has changed between a reference and a comparison scan.
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Inputs:
- Baseline .ply and Comparison .ply. Both start blank; in project mode, use 'Choose from project...' on each to pick between that side's Stage 3 (Cleanup) output and Stage 4 (Segment) output - the reference side can be the project's baseline, or an earlier scan; the comparison side is always a scan. Manual mode still has its own browse fields and registered-baseline dropdown.
- Registration RMS from Stage 3 (auto-fills when you pick a Comparison file via 'Choose from project...', reading that file's recorded icp_rms - stays editable afterward. Otherwise, type it in, or click 'Load from Stage 3', in manual mode)
- Normal scale / Search scale / Search depth
- M3C2 parameters .txt file - either generate one directly with 'Generate Params File...' (uses the four values above plus a confirmed-working reference for everything else), or browse to one made via CloudCompare's Plugins > M3C2 Distance dialog
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Outputs: Multiple .ply files - CloudCompare saves every loaded cloud, not just the M3C2 result. The result (the one with an M3C2 distance scalar field) is usually the sparser, more colorful-looking cloud; the others are unchanged copies of the input clouds. This is a known CloudCompare CLI quirk, not a setting we can turn off. In project mode, the applet detects the real result file and records it, along with the params file used and the registration error used, on the picked diff's own diff stage entry.
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).What to expect: A run report pops up after each successful run identifying which output is which. If generating the params file, remember Search scale and Search depth need to be set proportionally to Normal scale by hand - CloudCompare's own 'Guess params' doesn't update them automatically if you change Normal scale afterward, which caused a rounded/blunted-edges result in testing before this was caught.
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Next steps: Open the result cloud in CloudCompare, set its active scalar field to 'M3C2 distance', and check the color scale (red = positive change, blue = negative, magnitude = degree of change). Then use it as the input to Stage 6 (Classify).

Stage 6: Classify.Purpose: This stage removes scan noise from the M3C2 result. It keeps only the points that show real change. By default, it also groups the real-change points into separate damage sites, so a false-positive point with no neighbors does not count as damage.
Stage 6: Classify.Inputs:
- M3C2 diff result .ply (from Stage 5 - must have the distance scalar field; starts blank, use 'Choose from project...' to pick Stage 5's output, in project mode)
- Distance threshold in meters (or use 'Load RMS & Suggest Threshold' to compute one from Stage 3's saved registration RMS)
- Cluster settings (on by default): method (DBSCAN or HDBSCAN), cluster gap tolerance, cluster density, and minimum damage-site size. Turn clustering off to use the threshold alone, as before.
- Optional: keep all points and add flag fields instead of filtering, for inspection before committing
Stage 6: Classify.Outputs: By default, a .ply containing only the points that passed both the threshold and the clustering check (the distance field is preserved, so Stage 7's coloring still works unchanged). A 'cluster_id' field marks which damage site each point belongs to. With 'keep all' checked, every point is kept, with a 'classified' field (1 = passed the threshold, 0 = did not) and a 'cluster_id' field (-1 = not part of a confirmed site). When clustering is on, a matching '.clusters.json' file is also saved, listing each damage site's centroid, point count, size, and average/peak distance.
Stage 6: Classify.What to expect: The run report and tool output show how many points were flagged and what percentage that is - 0% usually means the threshold is too high, and close to 100% usually means it's too low. When clustering is on, the report also lists how many damage sites were found and how many flagged points were rejected as isolated noise. 'Load RMS & Suggest Threshold' looks up Stage 3's saved RMS sidecar (point it at the same comparison .ply used in Stage 5, not the M3C2 result itself) and multiplies by 2-3x as a starting point - only works if Stage 3 ran with alignment and successfully found an RMS value. If no damage sites survive clustering, lower the cluster density or minimum site size, or raise the cluster gap tolerance (DBSCAN only).
Stage 6: Classify.Next steps: If you used 'keep all', open the result in CloudCompare to see which points got flagged and which cluster they belong to, adjust the settings, and re-run. Otherwise, use the filtered output as the input to Stage 7 (Surface), or as the --change input to Stage 8 (Export) directly if a mesh is not needed.

Stage 7: Surface.Purpose: Reconstructs a triangle mesh from Stage 6's classified change cloud, using surface_reconstruction.py. A mesh reads more clearly than raw points in Omniverse, and also unlocks surface-area and volume figures for the flagged damage.
Stage 7: Surface.Inputs:
- Classified change cloud .ply (starts blank; use 'Choose from project...' to pick Stage 6's output, in project mode)
- Method: Poisson (a smooth continuous surface - good for room shells, walls, floors; tends to over-smooth cluttered scenes into blobs) or Ball Pivoting (stays closer to the real points - generally better for machinery or cluttered, thin geometry; more prone to holes where point density is uneven)
- [Poisson] Octree depth, density trim percentile
- [Ball Pivoting] Ball radii, comma-separated (leave blank to auto-estimate from the cloud's own point spacing)
- Carry field (defaults to 'M3C2 distance') - carries this scalar field from the input onto the mesh's vertices, so the mesh can still be colored by change magnitude in Stage 8. Requires scipy.
Stage 7: Surface.Outputs: A mesh .ply file. In project mode, this run's result is recorded on the picked diff's own surface stage entry.
Stage 7: Surface.What to expect: Check the tool output for vertex and triangle counts, and whether the mesh came out watertight. Zero triangles means reconstruction likely failed - check the input cloud has enough points and reasonable density. Which method suits a given change region is still an open question, worth checking visually after each run - Poisson and Ball Pivoting have both run successfully on real data, with Poisson producing a 'blobby' result on a dense, cluttered scan, which is the expected Poisson failure mode there, not a bug.
Stage 7: Surface.Next steps: Open the mesh in CloudCompare or Omniverse to check it visually, then use it as the --change input to Stage 8 (Export).

Stage 8: Export to USD.Purpose: Converts a cleaned baseline map and a change cloud or mesh into a USD scene for downstream use (e.g. Omniverse), with an optional .usdz package for web/AR/mobile viewers. Accepts either point clouds or meshes for either input independently.
Stage 8: Export to USD.Inputs:
- Path to a USD export script (defaults to usd_export.py next to the applet)
- Baseline .ply or mesh. Starts blank; in project mode, use 'Choose from project...' to pick the PROJECT's own baseline cleanup/segment output - not anything specific to the picked diff, since the exported scene's environment layer should stay the same no matter which diff produced the change highlight.
- Change-highlight .ply or mesh. Starts blank; in project mode, use 'Choose from project...' to pick the picked diff's own output (Diff, Classify, or Surface).
- Optional: damage detail .ply from extract_damage_detail.py. Not a tracked project stage - always picked by hand, in both manual and project mode.
- Output .usd path
- Optional: also package as .usdz
- Optional: downsample point cloud layers via voxel size (off by default)
Stage 8: Export to USD.Outputs: A .usd scene file with /World/Compartment/Baseline (muted grey, small points or a plain-colored mesh), /World/Compartment/ChangeHighlight (blue-white-red diverging colormap driven by the M3C2 distance field, larger points or a colored mesh if the field was carried through in Stage 7), and optionally /World/Compartment/DamageDetail (real comparison-cloud geometry near flagged locations, colored the same way - shows what damage/debris actually looks like now, since ChangeHighlight is a magnitude value plotted at baseline positions, not the true current shape). If the .usdz option is checked, also a matching .usdz package next to it.
Stage 8: Export to USD.What to expect: Requires 'pip install usd-core plyfile' in addition to the other packages. Point-cloud output has been confirmed valid (opened and read back successfully) including in Omniverse. Mesh input is fully supported and auto-detected - Stage 7 (Surface) is now a wired pipeline stage, so a mesh no longer has to come from running surface_reconstruction.py by hand. The DamageDetail layer (via extract_damage_detail.py) is new and hasn't been run against real data yet. If walls block the interior view in Omniverse, try Omniverse's camera near-clip distance to see through geometry the camera is positioned inside/behind, or toggle Baseline's visibility off in the Stage panel to isolate the other layers. Downsampling (if enabled) only affects point cloud layers, not meshes - it keeps one representative point per voxel cell, removing redundant near-duplicate points from overlapping scan passes rather than real detail, as long as the voxel size stays smaller than the smallest feature you care about seeing. Useful for reducing file size and processing load in viewers like Isaac Sim.
Stage 8: Export to USD.Next steps: Open the .usd file in Omniverse or any USD-compatible viewer, or the .usdz in a web/AR/mobile viewer, to check the scene looks right - baseline in muted grey, change regions colored by magnitude, and (if used) DamageDetail showing the real current shape.
